title: Volatility
body:
**Volatility** is the standard deviation of [[Financial Returns|returns]], and it is the
project's measure of risk. It is [[Variance]] from [[STATISTICS]] with no modification, so the
interpretation carries over: the typical distance of one day's return from the average day.

The convention is to report it annualised through [[Annualisation]]:

```
daily standard deviation of returns    1.2%
annualised                             1.2% × √252 = 19.05%
```

Higher volatility means wider swings in both directions, so a high-volatility asset is one
whose value a year out is less predictable. That is the whole content of the measure, and two
limitations follow from it.

**It is symmetric.** A 5% gain and a 5% loss contribute equally, and investors do not
experience them equally. Downside deviation is the variant that counts only losses.

**It assumes the past describes the future.** Volatility computed over a calm period
understates the risk of a violent one, which is why a [[Rolling Window]] is plotted
alongside the single number: the series shows volatility itself changing, and it spikes during
a crash and predicts none.

Market returns also have fatter tails than a [[Normal Distribution]], so extreme moves
happen more often than a standard deviation computed under that assumption suggests.
